description.purpose: An interactive canvas of the colony, reached at /<mount>/ on the colony's one listener. A timer takes a topology snapshot, a code cell turns it into display objects, and a `web` cell holds them and serves the page. The browser owns the drag and the camera; nothing else. Since 2.2.0 the refresh cadence is a LITERAL inside `./clock`'s `params.schedules` rather than a `CANVY_REFRESH_CRON` substitution token out of the colony's environment ([#138](https://github.com/mmeyerlein/meclaw/issues/138), ruling R-0904-6), so two canvases in one colony refresh at different cadences -- the environment form had one value for all of them.
description.use_when: Somebody should see and rearrange something the colony knows, in a browser. One canvy per canvas: two canvases are two hives under two mounts, which is what makes one reverse-proxy rule a complete access statement for one of them.
description.not_in_scope: It draws nothing the topology snapshot does not hold, and that snapshot arrives on a timer through this hive's OWN lane to the colony's read-only graph endpoint (GH #163), so the canvas is as fresh as that timer. No authentication and no TLS: since `canvy@2.3.0` the display owns no port at all -- it hangs on the colony's one listener under `override_params.web.mount` -- and whatever stands in front of that listener is somebody else's job (R-W8-2). No object library beyond cells, hives and edges. No interior address: `params.ports` is empty, so no cell in here is an endpoint -- a caller names the hive and a lane (in_refresh in, event out).
examples: GET http://127.0.0.1:7777/canvy/ -- the colony, draggable, arrangement persistent (7777 is the colony's own listener, /canvy/ the mount this template ships)
a drag -> object:set on the node's x and y -> a diff to every open browser, without one message entering the colony
every minute: a topology snapshot -> one bundle of object calls -> the picture catches up
